canopy.silhouette: flat-topped dense dark crown, thick leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds wrapped in bright orange-red arils are dropped by birds, often onto branches or rock crevices. The seedling has thick, glossy, paddle-shaped (obovate) leaves in opposite pairs like the adult, and on a host tree sends long aerial roots to the ground before becoming self-supporting. In the open it grows as a stout single-stemmed sapling.
growth.source: Pipoly & Graf / Flora of Ecuador and Colombia (Clusia multiflora: dioecious tree or hemiepiphyte 5-20 m in Andean and Central American montane forest, white to pink flowers with resin rewards, capsules splitting to show arillate seeds); growth and ages estimated from Clusia literature

fruiting.source: Clusia pollination studies (Bittrich & Amaral: resin-collecting bees incl. stingless bees on male and female flowers); Flora of Ecuador (Clusia multiflora many-flowered cymes, white to pink cup flowers; globose capsule opening by valves to show seeds in orange-red arils, bird-dispersed); timings estimated

canopy.silhouette: gnarled grey tree with a fine-textured crown

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-fine, hairy, wind-borne seeds sprout on moss and humus; the seedling has small opposite compound leaves with only a few leaflets on a winged midrib, the young shoots densely rusty-hairy. Saplings are slender and leafy, often leaning or forking low, and after cutting or fire they resprout into bushy multi-stemmed clumps; adult leaves carry many pairs of small leaflets.
growth.source: Wikipedia (EN/ES, Weinmannia tomentosa, encenillo): 15-25 m, trunk to 70 cm, 2500-3300 m in the Andes of Colombia and Venezuela, leaves 2-7 cm. Germination, growth rate, first flowering and lifespan estimated from cloud-forest trees of similar habit.

fruiting.source: Spanish Wikipedia (Weinmannia tomentosa): creamy-white flower spikes 4-6 cm, Aug-Nov; fruits Oct-Jan, small capsules that turn reddish and then caramel when ripe and open; seeds 1 mm with hairs for wind dispersal; pollinated by honeybees and tachinid flies. Flower counts, fruit set, hang, rot and crop estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling with tiny round cotyledons, then opposite, elliptic, leathery leaves with three strong curved veins from the base, as in the adult. It branches low into a small twiggy shrub of stiff paired leaves, often in forest edges and montane scrub, later a small, rounded tree.
growth.source: Estimated from Andean montane Miconia (Melastomataceae) shrubs and small trees: bird-dispersed berries, tiny light-germinating seeds, moderate growth; habit from Flora of Ecuador/Tropicos specimen descriptions

fruiting.source: Estimated from Andean Miconia: terminal panicles of small white 5-petalled flowers with poricidal anthers buzzed by bees and bumblebees; small blue-black many-seeded berries eaten by birds; flowering spread through the year near the equator

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-fine seeds sprout on wet moss or mossy banks in 1-3 weeks with two tiny round cotyledons. The seedling is a small succulent sprig of tiny, glossy, oval, finely toothed leaves in two rows; it branches from the base into arching, fern-like stems densely clothed in little leaves, with tiny white to pink flowers often within its first year.
growth.source: Wikipedia (shrub-like begonia to 1 m with succulent pendent stems ~45 cm clothed in small glossy oval leaves, small white flowers in panicles, no frost tolerance); germination and flowering times from general Begonia species culture; lifespan estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are minute, silvery-scaly tufts of narrow leaves that at first hold no water; as they grow the leaf bases widen into an upright, funnel-shaped, pale yellow-green tank rosette. It flowers once, a simple spike of white flowers in green bracts with dark stripes, topped by red-orange bracts, then makes pups and dies.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Guzmania monostachia: C3-CAM tank epiphyte of Florida, the Caribbean and the Andes); bromeliad horticulture and ecophysiology literature (monocarpic rosettes, simple striped spike with red tip, pups after flowering). Ages estimated.

epiphyte.name: Bird's nest fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate over 2-7 weeks into heart-shaped prothalli on wet bark and moss; 3-6 months after sowing tiny, simple, spoon- to strap-shaped, apple-green fronds appear. The young fern is a small open funnel of undivided glossy fronds with a dark midrib that widens year by year into a nest-like rosette catching leaf litter.
growth.source: Asplenium nidus developmental study (Am. J. Plant Sci., scirp.org): 47% of spores germinated by day 47, 100% by day 60, gametangia at 60-100 days; grower guides (Planet Natural); frond growth, first spores and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.name: Hanging moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores give a green, thread-like protonema on bark; small upright shoots follow as a thin golden-green fuzz on twigs. Shoots then lengthen and droop into slender, pendent, sparsely branched strands with tiny closely pressed leaves, golden-orange to yellow-brown, hanging in curtains from branches in wet forest.
growth.source: Estimated from pendent epiphytic mosses (Meteoriaceae) of humid Australasian forests: spore-to-shoot time and strand growth of a few cm a year inferred from hanging-moss growth studies; no species-specific data found

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators
